title: Combining complete and partial cell suppression methodologies in statistical disclosure control
contribution: A practitioner-venue note that sets classical (complete) and partial cell suppression side by side and proposes a combined MIP in which binaries gate the interval widths, so a statistical office can cap the number of intervals and impose minimum widths while keeping partial suppression's lower loss and built-in auditing; no algorithm is run for the combined model.
problem_entry: An attacker with any LP code turns a complete-suppression pattern into feasibility intervals, so the published output is already a table of intervals; the optimizer can choose the interval endpoints too (p. 3).
key_idea: Combined model: the partial-CSP LP in decrements and increments plus one binary per cell linked by z⁻ ≤ (a − lb)x and z⁺ ≤ (ub − a)x, so that a maximum number of intervals and a minimum width become linear constraints (pp. 5–6).
assumptions: Tables with linear links and attacker-known external bounds; lower, upper and sliding protection levels; fixed suppression costs for complete CSP and per-unit width costs for partial CSP (pp. 2, 4–5); the relation symbols of the models are lost in the text layer and read from S093 p. 8.
proof_devices: Protection requirements written as linear constraints by LP duality, details deferred to [1] and [3], pp. 5–6
Complexity contrast: complete CSP strongly NP-hard, partial CSP polynomial, combined model NP-hard in general, pp. 4, 6
experiments: One table taken from [1]: three real 2-D tables, partial vs complete loss (153 vs 486, 140,297 vs 281,398, 9,357 vs 19,099) and times (4.78–77.67 s vs 11.42–367.62 s plus 0.07–2,486.07 s of auditing) on a 'Pentium 133'; the losses are flagged as having different meanings; the combined model is not run (p. 4).
positioning: Unites the classical methodology (Willenborg and De Waal) with their own partial method [1], citing their Mathematical Programming 1999 and JASA 2000 papers for the algorithms (pp. 1–3, 5–6).
writing: Practitioner register: worked toy tables (Tables 1–4), advantages counted first, second and third, an exclamation ('but it is not!'), no proofs (pp. 2–4).
limits_future: The combined model is NP-hard and only claimed to be solvable by a branch-and-cut that 'can be implemented'; no computation for it and no future work stated (pp. 6–7).

method_links.note: The thinning happens in the problem definition: intervals instead of asterisks make the problem polynomial, and binaries return only to carry the office's controls.

The single table compares losses that the authors say mean different things; the commensurable weighting appears only in S093 (p. 8); the same times are attributed to a Pentium 133 here and to a Pentium/75 in S093 (pp. 7–8).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The intervals an attacker would compute by LP become the published decision variables, so the auditing phase disappears; see S093 pp. 2, 4.

transferable: When a requirement is checked by an LP that an adversary or auditor would solve, ask whether that LP's output can be the decision itself; here the published intervals are the variables and the auditing step disappears (pp. 3–4).

Merge a fixed-charge method and a continuous method into one MIP by gating each continuous width with a binary (z ≤ range·x), then write the operational controls (a count, a minimum width) as linear constraints on x and z (p. 6).

quotes.text: If the optimisation problem in classical (complete) cell suppression looks for cells to publish intervals instead of the exact original values, why not to look for the extreme values of the intervals too?
It looks like the optimisation problem of the new methodology (partial CSP) is more complicated than the old one (complete CSP), but it is not!

title: The generalized traveling salesman and orienteering problems
contribution: A survey chapter on cycle problems that combine node selection and sequencing, which restates with algorithmic detail and computation the authors' GTSP polytope and branch-and-cut papers and their orienteering branch-and-cut with conditional and branch cover cuts.
problem_entry: Cycle problems split into variants whose polytope contains the TSP polytope (simple lifting) and variants whose side constraints exclude tours (more involved constructions); the GTSP and the orienteering problem represent the two classes (pp. 3–11, 4).
key_idea: GTSP: lift TSP facets through intermediate polytopes P(F), separate generalized SECs exactly by max-flow and heuristically by spanning families, refine tours by layered shortest paths, initialize the root from a Lagrangian 1-tree; OP: cuts from the cycle and knapsack relaxations plus conditional cuts, and a two-stage branch-and-cut with branch cover cuts (pp. 14–31, 37–49).
assumptions: GTSP: complete undirected graph, clusters partitioning the nodes (m ≥ 3; m ≥ 5 for the polyhedral results), triangular integer costs in the computations, E-GTSP polynomial for fixed m; OP: nonnegative prizes, edge durations, time bound t₀ = ⌈α·v(TSP)⌉, a depot (pp. 9, 12–13, 27–28, 36, 50).
proof_devices: Dimension of P(F) by induction on |F| with an extra Hamiltonian cycle per released node, Theorem 1, p. 14
Sequential lifting (Padberg) of any TSP facet into a GTSP facet, Theorem 3, p. 15
Rank of the v-compatibility graph bounds the face dimension (Lemma 7), and tight-triangular inequalities supply its edges (Lemma 9), pp. 18–20
Validity of path inequalities by contradiction on a feasible solution containing the path plus an edge to a node outside W(P), p. 40
Tooth-overlap simplification of 2-matching cuts that never decreases the violation, p. 43
Matroid argument: the SECs active at a maximum spanning tree are the ones needed, so Kruskal's components give a family likely to be violated, p. 24
experiments: GTSP (from the 1997 paper): 27 TSPLIB-derived instances with 137–442 nodes on an HP 9000/720 with CPLEX 2.1, all solved, about half without branching, grid clusterings harder; OP: four classes up to 500 nodes on an HP Apollo 9000/720 with CPLEX 3.0 and a 5-hour limit, the Laporte–Martello code rerun on the same machine, instances from the rivals' generators, Gendreau–Laporte–Semet compared at a limit converted by a published speed factor (pp. 32–36, 49–56).
positioning: A self-review: the GTSP section is 'mainly based on' FST [25] and [26], the OP section on [27]; the Laporte–Martello branch-and-bound and the concurrent Gendreau–Laporte–Semet branch-and-cut are compared directly (pp. 13, 37, 52–56).
writing: Survey register with procedures given in detail and their parameter values (5 LPs, 1000/50 subgradient iterations, 15 strong-branching candidates); claims hedged ('typically performs better than (although does not dominate)'); an erratum printed (pp. 28–30, 48–50).
limits_future: No polyhedral analysis of the OP exists (p. 37); some OP instances hit the time limit and one random 500-node instance is unsolved (pp. 52, 54); the two-stage scheme does not dominate (p. 49); no conclusions or future work (p. 56).

method_links.note: The rival's code is run on the authors' machine, the rivals' own generators make Classes III and IV, and where only published times exist the limit is converted with a published speed factor and both solved counts are printed.

Slow cutting-plane convergence is blamed on selecting cuts by individual violation; the cure is a separation round that returns a family spanning the graph (argued on the shortest spanning tree problem). It changes what each round returns, not where the loop queries.
Step 4 (measure the ceiling) applied to a bounding component: the LP bound of the simplified model shows that the Lagrangian bound's 11.6% gap is the model's, not the subgradient method's.
Projection decided by LP density: the y variables stay in the LP and are projected out only for the Lagrangian.
The survey prints an erratum of their own 1998 prize definition for Generation 2; a correction, not a re-test.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Cuts valid only for improving solutions
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Conditional cuts need to hold only for solutions better than the incumbent; branch cover cuts may cut off the optimum and are made safe by storing the support graphs they exclude and rerunning branch-and-cut on their union.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Reduce to the known special case and lift (existing)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The TSP polytope is a face of the GTSP polytope, and facets are lifted one released node at a time (restating S030).
OP cuts from the cycle relaxation (logical, 2-matching) and from the knapsack relaxation of the time constraint (covers), path inequalities from both.

transferable: Return a nested family of subtour-type cuts per separation round (the components Kruskal's algorithm builds on the x* weights) rather than the individually most violated ones (pp. 24–25).

Use cuts that need only hold for solutions better than the incumbent, e.g. x(E(S)) ≤ y(S) − 1 when the prizes in S cannot beat it, or the support-graph cut once the support graph has been enumerated within a time limit (pp. 40–41, 45).
If a cut may remove the optimum, store what it excludes, finish the root, and rerun branch-and-cut on the union of the stored graphs with that cut disabled (pp. 48–49).
Start the root LP from the constraints active in the best Lagrangian solution, so the first LP bound is at least the Lagrangian bound (p. 30).
To decide whether a weak bound is the method's or the model's fault, compute the LP bound of the same model next to it (p. 33).

Against rival codes: run their code on your machine when you have it, generate instances with their generator, and when only published times exist convert the time limit with a published speed factor and report both counts (pp. 50, 52, 54, 56).

quotes.text: In order to speed up the convergence of the cutting plane phase, instead, for each round of separation it is advisable to produce a family of violated inequalities “spanning” the overall graph.
Therefore, any inequality can be exploited as a cutting plane, provided that it is satisfied by every feasible OP solution of value greater than LB.

title: Exact methods for the asymmetric traveling salesman problem
contribution: A survey of exact ATSP methods (AP-based branch-and-bound, the Fischetti–Toth additive bound, the Fischetti–Toth branch-and-cut) with a new common comparison of four codes, Concorde on transformed instances included, on 86 instances, in which every code is tuned and the authors' own codes' losses are printed.
problem_entry: What exact ATSP methods appeared after the Balas–Toth survey, and how they compare on one machine with the best symmetric TSP code applied through ATSP-to-STSP transformations (p. 3).
key_idea: Relaxations (AP, r-arborescence, anti-arborescence and degree-constrained versions) organize three families: AP-based branch-and-bound, an additive chain that passes reduced costs from relaxation to relaxation (with a shortest-path bias of the AP duals), and a branch-and-cut with ATSP-specific separation, 1-arc shrinking and AP pricing (pp. 4–28).
assumptions: Complete digraph with nonnegative integer costs; 86 instances from Cirasella et al., Balas, two real-world instances, random costs in [1, 1000] and TSPLIB, available on request (pp. 4, 28–30).
proof_devices: Additive bounding validity by induction over residual cost matrices with two conditions per procedure, p. 11
Alternative optimal AP dual u − L, v + L from shortest-path potentials, biasing path costs toward the next relaxation, pp. 14–15
Transposition: a valid inequality's transpose is valid for the transposed point, so one separator serves both classes, p. 19
Minimum-weight odd cycle through an edge by shortest paths in a doubled bipartite graph (Gerards–Schrijver), pp. 20–21
Face argument for shrinking: separating x* from P equals separating it from any face whose inequality x* satisfies with equality; 1-arc faces of the ATSP are again ATSP polytopes, pp. 22–23
AP pricing bound Z + Δ_AP ≤ z ≤ Z from a Lagrangian reading of the LP duals, p. 25
experiments: Four codes (CDT, FT-add, FT-b&c, Concorde through 2- and 3-node transformations) on one Digital Alpha 533 MHz with CPLEX 6.5.3, 86 instances; a tuning paragraph per code (Fractionality Persistency for FT-b&c; Concorde's transformation, chunk sizes 0–32 and a fixed seed); 1,000 s for the branch-and-bound codes and 10,000 s for the branch-and-cut codes with the reason given; root, final LB and UB gaps, nodes, time (pp. 29–39).
positioning: Covers work after Balas–Toth; compares CDT with Miller–Pekny only by their published results ('comparable'); credits Lobel's Lagrangian pricing as an independent relative of AP pricing; treats Concorde as the strong rival and explains its robustness (pp. 3, 10, 25, 39).
writing: Losses discussed in the text with explanations ('Strangely enough', 'Not surprisingly') and 'In our view' hedges; a code-tuning section placed before the comparison (pp. 29–39).
limits_future: FT-b&c is built for medium instances (up to 200 vertices) without sophisticated primal heuristics or tuned LP interfaces and fails on crane316.10; future: ATSP-specific cuts such as lifted cycle inequalities, and ATSP-specific separation added to Concorde (pp. 34, 39).

method_links.note: One machine and LP solver; the rival tuned as carefully as his own codes, its default kept because best; his own losses printed (FT-add never best, FT-b&c's failure); unequal time limits justified by preliminary runs.
Step 2: the model that fits is the original directed one; FT-b&c's root bounds dominate Concorde's pure STSP version on the transformed instances. Nothing is removed from the model.
B-ADD-ATSP keeps the bounding procedures and changes what the chain hands to the next one (a biased alternative optimal dual); the step looks weaker but lets the next step add more.
His own 1992 and 1997 codes are re-run ten years later against the newest rival on a common machine, with improvements added; no earlier claim is named and tested.
A seed is fixed only for reproducibility, and FT-b&c's failure is attributed, untested, to an unlucky sequence of early branching choices.
Existing tools reused as black boxes (STSP separators, transposition); the closing advice is to add ATSP-specific separation to the general STSP code.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The ATSP additive chain AP → 1-SAP → 1-SAAP → r-SADP/r-SAADP and its shortest-path-biased version.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Chvátal–Gomory derivation as validity proof and separation handle (existing)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Odd CAT separation as a specialized version of the Caprara–Fischetti separation of a subclass of Chvátal–Gomory cuts.

transferable: In an additive bounding chain, choose among alternative optimal duals the one that biases the residual costs toward what the next relaxation needs (here shortest-path potentials from the root), even if that step adds nothing itself (pp. 14–15).
Reuse a separator for a transposed or symmetric inequality class by transforming x* on input and the cut on output (pp. 16, 19).
Before shrinking a set for separation, check that the face it induces corresponds one to one with a smaller instance: 1-arcs qualify for the ATSP, 1-edges do not for the STSP (pp. 22–23).
Strengthen the pricing test with a cheap combinatorial relaxation on the reduced costs (an assignment problem, bound Z + Δ_AP) and switch to it only when many columns price out wrongly (pp. 25–26).
In a code comparison, give every code, the rival included, its own tuning paragraph, fix seeds, and write down why the time limits differ (pp. 29–34).

quotes.text: Code FT-add has, on average, better performance than CDT (solving to optimality, within 1,000 CPU seconds, 8 more instances), never being, however, the best of the four codes on any instance.
The smaller time limit given to the first two algorithms is chosen so as to keep the required search-tree space reasonable, but it does not affect the comparison with the other algorithms

title: Exact algorithms for minimum routing cost trees
contribution: An exact branch-and-price-and-cut for the minimum routing cost tree with a path formulation, a new combinatorial bound and 'LP shortcutting' (preemptive branching and fathoming from intermediate column/row-generation bounds, 44% mean saving), which solves Euclidean instances up to 30 and random ones up to 40 vertices in an hour, plus a routing-cost-tree alignment heuristic that cuts the alignment cost by about 6% against Gusfield's star.
problem_entry: The minimum routing cost spanning tree is NP-hard even in the metric case and only approximation results existed; exact algorithms are the target, and Wu et al.'s suggestion that low routing-cost trees beat Gusfield's star alignment gives an application (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Path formulation with Dijkstra pricing and run-time rows; LP shortcutting uses the column phases' lower limit and the row phases' upper limit on the node bound to branch (l″ < u) or fathom (l′ ≥ u) before the LP is solved, and truncates column generation after six phases (pp. 2–6).
assumptions: Undirected graphs with nonnegative lengths; Euclidean and random, complete, dense or sparse test graphs, complete Euclidean the hardest; PRINTS protein families with 10–20 sequences of 200–600 amino acids (pp. 2, 9, 12).
proof_devices: Integrality needed only on edge variables, since a tree fixes one path per pair, p. 3
Pricing as a shortest path per pair with costs d + v, p. 3
Equivalence of the path and multicommodity flow formulations by flow decomposition, p. 3
Combinatorial bound l_COMB via a maximum spanning tree on the savings δ(i, j), improving Dionne–Florian's, p. 4
Lower and upper limits l′ ≤ l ≤ l″ from column and row phases, monotone in the iterations, p. 5
MST-based upper bound on an edge's load for node tightening, p. 6
Validity of (23) from its tightness only when one endpoint is a leaf, p. 7
experiments: C with CPLEX 5.0 on a Pentium Celeron 300 MHz; settings chosen one factor at a time; bounds normalized to l_IP1; rival bound reimplemented; one-instance degeneracy trace; LP shortcutting on 100 hard instances (mean saving 44%); 210 graphs with 1-hour limit (Euclidean to 30 vertices, random to 40, rarely 50); edge-weight-range experiment on 100 instances; alignment on PRINTS (about 6% better than the best star) (pp. 9–13).
positioning: Improves Dionne–Florian's bound and reimplements it to show its weakness; extends Wong's and Gusfield's star-based results from stars to minimum routing cost trees; cites Wu et al.'s PTAS (pp. 2, 4, 9–10).
writing: Contribution list in the introduction; novelty hedged ('to the best of our knowledge'); a one-factor-at-a-time computational narrative with normalized tables; some results left to a technical report (pp. 2, 5, 7, 9–11).
limits_future: Exact solution stops at about 30–40 vertices in an hour on a slow PC, beyond which the bound certifies solutions within 1% on average; extension to minimum communication cost networks and to new alignment programs (p. 13).

method_links.note: The column-generation loop is traced on one 20-vertex instance and fixed at loop level (row generation for smaller, less degenerate LPs, alternation, truncation after six phases), while the Dijkstra pricing oracle stays. A column-generation loop, not a cut loop.
Step 5 (credit the lineage): intermediate bounds for fathoming are credited as known; only preemptive branching is claimed as new.
Step 1: the rival Dionne–Florian bound is reimplemented and run in the same code on the same machine instead of being quoted.
The spread is instance hardness, not run-to-run variability; it is noticed and turned into a designed factor (edge-weight ranges, 10 classes of 10 instances). No seeds.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Lower bound as an audit of a heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Beyond the solvable size the formulations certify local-search solutions within 1% of optimality on average after an hour; also S135.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Facets of a small aggregate by enumeration and PORTA
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The extreme feasible vectors of (L_ij, D_i, D_j, x_ij) are enumerated, their convex-hull facets computed with PORTA for several n, and a general valid inequality derived.

transferable: In branch-and-price with row and column generation, track l′ after each column phase and l″ after each row phase; branch when l″ < u and fathom when l′ ≥ u, unless the gap to the incumbent is below a threshold (0.5% here) (pp. 5–6).
Keep the branching variables permanently in the LP and price out only the others, so branching never conflicts with pricing (p. 3).
Print a table of bound against time per column-generation phase and truncate where the tail starts (here six phases give about 99% of the bound) (pp. 5, 11).
Find candidate inequalities for a small aggregate of variables by enumerating its feasible extreme vectors and running PORTA for several sizes, then prove the general form (p. 7).
Measure a node-level speed-up over the whole tree, since work saved at one node can be needed later (p. 5).

quotes.text: Although the idea of using intermediate bounds for fathoming the node is known, the use of preemptive branching is (to the best of our knowledge) new.

It is worth noting that at a single node the speed up can be greater than 90%; however, the work saved at a node (e.g., generation of useful columns) may be needed at a later time, so the overall saving is less impressive than the one obtained, for example, at the root node.

title: Polyhedral theory for the asymmetric traveling salesman problem
contribution: A survey of ATSP-specific polyhedral results by Balas and Fischetti: monotonization and facet transfer (answering a Grötschel–Padberg research problem), sequence-independent lifting procedures, canonical forms for facet equivalence, and the odd CAT, source-destination and lifted cycle classes, including rank-1 members and members of unbounded Chvátal rank.
problem_entry: The ATS polytope deserves study on its own: it subsumes the STSP, is far richer (35 of 319,015 facets of P₆ are symmetric), models real sequencing problems, informs the STSP, and the STSP reduction doubles the nodes and has a special structure (pp. 3, 5).
key_idea: Organize the ATSP-specific facet theory around a few general devices: full-dimensional monotonization with transfer conditions, closed-form clique lifting and related liftings, canonical forms, and the characterization of 2-liftable chord sets for lifted cycle inequalities (pp. 13–47).
assumptions: Complete loop-free digraph on n ≥ 5 nodes, the Dantzig–Fulkerson–Johnson formulation, the ATS polytope and its monotonization; separation not addressed (pp. 3–5).
proof_devices: Facet proof by induction on the number of clones with affinely independent tours built explicitly, Theorem 3.3, pp. 17–18
Support-reducedness equals connectivity of the bipartite graph B[G₀], Theorem 2.8, p. 15; three isolated nodes in G⁺ suffice for a facet of P, Corollary 2.10, p. 16
Validity by rank-1 Chvátal derivations (odd CAT Remark 5.4, p. 29; SD Theorem 6.1, p. 31; T-lifting, p. 20)
Validity by a case split on x(Q₁) ≥ 1 with degree inequalities added and, for odd cycle lengths, halving and rounding, pp. 44–46
A fractional point satisfying degree and subtour constraints but violating the inequality by more than 1 certifies Chvátal rank above 1, p. 40
Unbounded Chvátal rank: exponentially many SECs need positive multipliers in any derivation (Chvátal–Cook–Hartmann), Theorem 7.11, p. 42
positioning: Starts from what Grötschel and Padberg's 1985 survey knew and answers its research problem on monotone versus flat facets; relates clique lifting to Padberg–Rinaldi clique-liftability and Naddef–Rinaldi 0-node lifting; cites Queyranne–Wang for symmetric inequalities (pp. 5, 8, 16, 19–20).
writing: Survey register: each section names its source papers ([4], [13], [6]); full proofs only for central theorems, others referred to the sources; a verbatim quotation of the research problem being answered (pp. 16–18, 27, 29, 31, 35).
limits_future: Separation is left to other chapters; most proofs are in the cited papers; no conclusions or open questions (the chapter ends with Corollary 7.16) (pp. 4–5, 47).

method_links.note: Polyhedral, not computational: the case for staying in the original directed space instead of transforming to the STSP; the theory behind S056's computational finding (S056 p. 34).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Reduce to the known special case and lift (existing)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Facets carried from smaller graphs by cloning nodes into cliques with closed-form, sequence-independent coefficients; T-lifting, merge lifting and 2-cycle cloning.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Chvátal–Gomory derivation as validity proof and separation handle (existing)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Rank-1 derivations prove odd CAT and SD validity; Chvátal rank classifies lifted cycle inequalities (rank-1 classes, unbounded rank).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Prove in the full-dimensional relaxation, then transfer back
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Monotonization removes the equations that complicate interchange arguments, and simple graph conditions carry its facets back to the ATS polytope.

transferable: Before using sequential lifting, look for a lifting with closed-form, sequence-independent coefficients (clique lifting: δ_k = max{α_ik + α_kj − α_ij}) (pp. 16–19).

Prove facets in the full-dimensional monotone polytope, where interchange arguments are short, then transfer them with an easy sufficient condition (three nodes isolated in the support graph G⁺ of the nonzero coefficients, Corollary 2.10) (pp. 13–16).
Put inequalities into a canonical form before claiming that a family is new or that two members differ (pp. 24–26, 34).
To show that an inequality is not of Chvátal rank 1, exhibit a point that satisfies the degree and subtour elimination constraints but violates the inequality by more than 1 (p. 40).

quotes.text: But the symmetric inequalities obtained this way define only a tiny fraction of the multitude of facets of the ATS polytope, the vast majority of the latter being defined by asymmetric inequalities that have no counterpart for the STS polytope defined on G.
This gives an unexpectedly simple answer to an open problem posed by Gr¨otschel and Padberg

title: Partial cell suppression: a new methodology for statistical disclosure control
contribution: Introduces partial cell suppression (publish intervals instead of missing cells), shows that its optimization is an LP solvable in polynomial time after a Benders-type projection of the attacker certificates into capacity cuts, and reports a preliminary three-instance comparison in which a restricted version loses 31–50% of the information complete suppression loses and needs no separate auditing.
problem_entry: Complete cell suppression is strongly NP-hard and the attacker computes each hidden cell's range by LP anyway; publish intervals instead, for a smaller loss, polynomial solvability and free auditing ranges (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: Model the published decrements and increments as LP variables and replace the per-cell certificate tables (over 10^7 variables for a 100×100 table) by capacity cuts obtained from the LP duals of the attacker subproblems, separated in a cutting-plane loop (pp. 3–6).
assumptions: Any table My = b with attacker-known external bounds (k-dimensional, linked, hierarchical; network structure only for k = 2); lower, upper and sliding protection levels; nonnegative weights, under which the optimal ranges equal the auditing ranges (pp. 3–4).
proof_devices: LP duality of the attacker subproblem turns the existence of a certifying table into the cut family Σ(α z⁺ + β z⁻) ≥ z⁺ over the dual extreme points, pp. 4–6
Ma = b removes the nominal values from the cuts, p. 5
Polynomial solvability by the equivalence of optimization and separation, p. 6
Nonnegative weights make the optimal ranges minimal, hence equal to the attacker's auditing ranges, p. 4
experiments: Restricted model (z⁺ = UB x, z⁻ = LB x, possibly worse optimum) solved by their complete-CSP code with integrality features off and stopped at the root, Pentium/75 with CPLEX 3.0, three real 2-D instances, complete-CSP weights set to the a priori interval width for comparability: partial loss 31–50% of complete loss, times 4.78–77.67 s vs 367.69–2,603.00 s including auditing (pp. 7–8).
positioning: Reviews CSP heuristics (Cox, Sande, Kelly–Golden–Assad, Carvalho et al.), Kelly's huge MILP and Geurts' refinement, and their own exact methods of 1999 and 2000 (p. 2).
writing: Three advantages announced in the introduction and repeated in the conclusion; the computation labelled preliminary; 'exponential complexity' used loosely for the strongly NP-hard classical problem (pp. 2, 7–8).
limits_future: Computation preliminary and on a slight modification of the model (p. 8); future: fixed penalties for replaced entries with 0-1 variables, a maximum count and minimum widths, unifying complete and partial suppression (the combined model of S180) (p. 8).

method_links.note: Step 3: the auxiliary certificate tables are projected out Benders-style, leaving a model in the published widths only; unlike the 1999 paper (s01 card S069) this one names Benders.

Losses made commensurable by the complete-CSP weights; auditing time counted in the classical arm; the new method run in a restricted version whose optimum can only be worse, so (my reading) the savings shown are a lower bound.
Step 3: the smallest code is the authors' own branch-and-cut with integrality features off and stopped at the root, not a general-purpose MIP solver.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The attacker's LP ranges are the published intervals, and at an optimum they coincide with the auditing ranges; see S180 pp. 3–4.

transferable: Replace per-scenario certificate variables (one auxiliary solution per sensitive cell) by cuts in the master variables derived from the dual of each scenario LP, separated by solving that LP at the master point (pp. 4–6).
Let preprocessing and pool initialization share one pass: evaluate each requirement at a trivial solution, drop those already met, and store the dual cut of each of the others in the pool (p. 7).
Before comparing two methods whose objectives measure different things, choose weights that make the measures commensurable and state the choice in the setup (p. 8).

quotes.text: We next derive an equivalent model inspired by Benders’ decomposition (see e.g. Nemhauser and Wolsey (1988)), which is based on the same technique we used in Fischetti and Salazar (2000) in the context of complete CSP.
This produces complete CSP instances which can fairly be compared with their corresponding partial CSP versions.

title: Optimisation of the interconnecting network of a UMTS radio mobile telephone system
contribution: A MILP with logical, generalized-cover and trivial strengthening constraints and a MINTO/CPLEX branch-and-cut for designing a three-level UMTS interconnection network, used on 14 CSELT instances to certify the partner's tabu search (gaps 0.68–7.12% after 2 hours) and compared against CPLEX 5.0 and 7.0 as black boxes.
problem_entry: An industrial three-level star network design problem (strongly NP-hard, generalizing facility location) from CSELT; the computation's goal is to judge the partner's tabu search, with the LP bound as a yardstick for practitioners' solutions (pp. 3–4, 6, 8).
key_idea: A MILP with 0-1 opening and assignment variables, integer module counts and continuous flows, strengthened by logical constraints and generalized cover inequalities on each CSS's modules, separated as 0-1 knapsacks inside a branch-and-cut that generates even model rows dynamically (pp. 4–9).
assumptions: Traffic, channels and modules per BTS; capacitated CSSs of two types and LEs; BTS types basic, isolated or free; forbidden connections removed; hardness from the interaction of 0-1 and integer module variables; 14 CSELT instances with 85–120 BTSs (pp. 3–6, 9).
proof_devices: Two-case validity argument for the generalized cover inequality (17), p. 7
Separation of (17) reduced to a minimization 0-1 knapsack for fixed d, with item fixing (zero cost) and removal (cost at least 1 − g*/d), pp. 7–8
Restriction of the separation to d = ⌈g*⌉, justified by experience, p. 8

title: A local branching heuristic for mixed‐integer programs with 2‐level variables, with an application to a telecommunication network design problem
contribution: DRT, a variable-neighbourhood local-branching heuristic built around black-box CPLEX that detects first-level binaries automatically and explores nested neighbourhoods with the first level fixed, reported better than CPLEX 7.0, original local branching and an ablation without first-level variables on 20 UMTS instances (with ties, one run each).
problem_entry: The original local branching did worse than CPLEX on the UMTS instances; that failure motivated a variant that detects and exploits two-level structure (pp. 1, 3, 14).
key_idea: Express VNS and tabu ingredients as linear constraints for a black-box MIP: refine with first-level variables fixed, tight-refine on second-level rings, diversify to a first feasible solution within a first-level distance band, forbid revisits statically (pp. 3–6).
assumptions: MIP with a nonempty binary set; first-level variables found by a logical-dependency slack criterion or a big-M criterion (bigM_perc = 5), or supplied by the modeller; UMTS test bed of 20 instances from S135's model (pp. 2, 8–9, 12).
proof_devices: Maximum-slack argument: if |α_j|(UB_j − LB_j) ≥ δ_max for a binary with α_j < 0, setting it to 0 forces all other variables of the row to their bounds, p. 8
Big-M reasoning: a tiny fractional y satisfies a big-M row in the LP, so fixing y strongly affects solvability, pp. 7–8
experiments: Pentium III/1 GHz, CPLEX 7.0 as black box, one 3-hour run per instance on UMTS-1 to UMTS-20; DRT vs CPLEX (MIPEmphasis 1), DRT2, DRT with no first-level variables, local branching at its paper's UMTS setting; δ and δ%; a preliminary table from Polo's thesis (Pentium III/350 MHz) vs VNS, CPLEX and problem-specific tabu search, where DRT loses on UMTS-3; no seeds (pp. 9, 12–14).
positioning: Builds on Fischetti–Lodi local branching (its concluding remark) and on VNS and tabu search; compares with the problem-specific tabu search of a 1997 Padova master's thesis and with Polo's 2002 thesis implementation (pp. 1–3, 12).
writing: Claims at full strength ('better heuristic solutions than the alternative methods on all the instances') against a table with ties; implementation effort (lines of code) as an argument; pseudo-code and parameter files in appendices (pp. 2, 12, 14, 18–23).
limits_future: One application class, ties and DRT2 wins on large instances (pp. 9, 14); future: other network design problems and more powerful first-level detection (p. 16).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: First-level variables are found automatically from row slacks and big-M coefficients and drive a structure-specific neighbourhood scheme inside a general MIP heuristic.

transferable: Detect 'first-level' binaries automatically: a binary with a negative coefficient whose range covers the row's maximum slack forces the other variables to their bounds when set to 0; a coefficient above 5 times the row's average flags a big-M switch (p. 8).

Write intensification and diversification as constraints around a black-box MIP: fix the first level, explore second-level rings of growing radius, diversify to a first feasible solution within a band of first-level distance, and forbid revisits with a static Δ₁ ≥ 1 cut (pp. 4–6).
Include an ablation arm that removes the key structural ingredient, and the solver's heuristic-emphasis setting as a baseline (pp. 13–14).
Put the pseudo-code and the exact parameter files in an appendix (pp. 18–23).

quotes.text: The metaheuristic scheme is then built on top of a general-purpose MIP solver, which is used as a black box to explore solution neighborhoods defined by the original MIP model amended by suitable local branching cuts.

As a matter of fact, the unsatisfactory performance of the original Local Branching scheme on UMTS instances gave us motivation to investigate a Local Branching variant capable of detecting automatically (and exploiting) certain relevant MIP structures, thus originating the research reported in the present paper.
